description.en: The 1 2 stick drill is a footwork and conditioning drill commonly used in athletic warm ups. Two quick steps are followed by a balanced stick landing, sharpening reaction and lower body control.

en: Stand tall with feet hip width apart in an athletic stance.
Drop into a quarter squat with hands ready in front.
Step quickly with one foot forward, then the other foot.
On the second step, plant the foot and freeze in a stable stick.
Hold the stick position with knees soft and chest up.
Reset to the start and repeat the 1 2 step pattern in another direction.
Stay light on the balls of the feet throughout.
Continue the drill for the desired duration.
Improves footwork and reaction speed.
Builds single leg balance through the stick landing.
Strengthens ankle and knee stabilizers.
Trains controlled deceleration like an athlete.
Excellent warm up before sport or lifting.

description.en: The alternating step out is a side-stepping bodyweight move where the lifter steps one foot out wide to the side and lowers into a lateral lunge then steps back to the start. The pattern alternates sides for a strong lateral hip and glute builder.

en: Stand tall with feet together and arms at your sides.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Step one foot out wide to the side.
Bend the knee on the stepping leg into a lateral lunge.
Keep the trail leg straight with the foot flat on the floor.
Push back through the working leg heel to return to the start.
Bring the foot back to the standing position.
Alternate sides each rep.
Builds lateral hip strength
Trains the adductors
No equipment needed
Easy to scale
Useful warm-up move
Strong glute medius work

description.en: The back relaxation pose (constructive rest position) is a simple restorative position where you lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. It allows the lower back to release naturally without active stretching, decompresses the spine, and is one of the most effective interventions for back tension and recovery.

en: Lie on your back on the floor or a mat.
Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart.
Position your feet so your knees fall comfortably toward each other or stack directly above your feet — whichever is more comfortable.
Place your hands on your belly or rest them at your sides with palms up.
Close your eyes. Relax your jaw, shoulders, and hips.
Allow the floor to support your weight completely. Let go of any muscle tension.
Breathe naturally and deeply. Stay in the position for 5 to 20 minutes.
To exit, slowly roll to one side and rise gently.
Releases back tension naturally
Decompresses the spine
Restorative — useful as a cool-down or recovery practice
Reduces stress
No equipment needed
Easy to integrate into any routine

description.en: The band close grip biceps curl is performed with the hands held closer than shoulder-width to bias the long head of the biceps. The narrow grip places more emphasis on the inner portion of the upper arm. The band gives increasing tension at the top of the curl for a strong contraction.

en: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart.
Hold a handle in each hand with hands closer than shoulder-width.
Use an underhand grip with palms forward.
Brace your core and keep your chest up.
Curl the handles up toward your shoulders.
Keep your elbows pinned at your sides.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the handles slowly back to the start.
Targets the biceps long head
Builds the inner upper arm
Increasing tension at the top
Strong peak contraction
Easy to set up at home
Useful for arm shape and detail

description.en: The band close-grip pulldown is a lat pulldown variation using a resistance band with a narrow, close grip. The close grip shifts more emphasis to the biceps and lower lats compared to a wide grip. It is an effective at-home pulling exercise.

en: Anchor a resistance band at a high point overhead.
Kneel or stand facing the anchor. Grip the band with both hands close together (6 to 12 inches apart).
Start with arms extended overhead.
Pull the band down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back.
Squeeze your lats and biceps at the bottom.
Slowly extend back overhead under control.
Keep your torso upright throughout.
Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Close grip emphasizes biceps and lower lats
Mimics close-grip lat pulldown at home
Highly portable
Easy to scale by band thickness
Builds pulling strength
Useful when no cable machine is available

description.en: The band kneeling preacher curl combines a preacher pad with a resistance band for strict bicep work. Kneeling behind the preacher bench with arms over the pad, you curl the band ends with both hands. The preacher pad eliminates body english while the band provides constant tension.

en: Anchor a resistance band to a low point in front of a preacher bench.
Kneel behind the preacher bench with chest pressed to the pad.
Grip the band ends with both hands using an underhand grip.
Drape your arms over the preacher pad with arms fully extended.
Brace your core and pin your chest to the pad.
Curl the band up by bending only at the elbows.
Squeeze the biceps hard at the top.
Lower the band back down with control to full extension.
Strict bicep isolation
Eliminates body english
Constant band tension through the range
Useful for home training
Strong stretch at the bottom
Builds bicep size with peak contraction

description.en: The band kneeling pulldown mimics a cable lat pulldown by anchoring a resistance band overhead and pulling it down while kneeling. The kneeling position prevents body english, keeping the movement strict. It is an effective at-home lat exercise.

en: Anchor a resistance band at a high point overhead (pull-up bar, top of door frame).
Kneel on the floor facing the anchor. Grip both ends of the band with palms facing forward.
Start with arms extended overhead, band taut.
Pull the band down by driving your elbows down and back toward your ribs.
Squeeze your lats at the bottom of the pull.
Slowly extend your arms back overhead under control.
Maintain an upright torso throughout.
Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Mimics lat pulldown at home
Kneeling prevents cheating
Builds the lats and biceps
Highly portable
Easy to scale by band thickness
Useful when no cable machine is available

description.en: The band reverse curl uses a resistance band with an overhand (pronated) grip to target the brachioradialis and forearm extensors — the muscles on top of the forearm. It builds forearm size and grip strength with minimal equipment.

en: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart.
Grip both ends of the band with palms facing down (overhand/pronated grip).
Stand tall. Pin your elbows at your sides.
Curl both ends of the band upward by bending at the elbows.
Continue until your forearms are parallel to the floor or higher.
Squeeze the top of your forearms at the peak.
Lower under control over two seconds. Maintain the overhand grip throughout.
Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Targets the brachioradialis and forearm extensors
Builds forearm size and grip
Highly portable
Easy to scale by band thickness
Useful when no dumbbells are available
Joint-friendly

description.en: The barbell curl press extension is an arm complex that links three exercises into one fluid movement. You curl the barbell to the shoulders, press it overhead, then perform an overhead triceps extension behind your head, before reversing the chain back to the start. The complex hits the entire arm in a single rep.

en: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a barbell with an underhand grip about shoulder-width.
Begin with the bar resting at your thighs, arms fully extended.
Curl the bar up to shoulder height by bending at the elbows, keeping your upper arms still.
From the top of the curl, press the bar straight overhead until your arms are fully extended.
Lower the bar behind your head by bending only at the elbows, performing an overhead triceps extension.
Press the bar back overhead by extending your elbows.
Lower the bar to shoulder height, then reverse the curl to bring the bar back down to your thighs.
That is one rep. Continue with smooth, controlled motion through the full complex.
Hits biceps, shoulders, and triceps in one efficient sequence
Builds coordination across multiple movement patterns
Time-efficient arm training
Improves shoulder mobility through the overhead positions
Strong cardiovascular component when performed continuously
Excellent finisher for upper body sessions

description.en: The barbell front chest squat holds the bar against the chest with both arms wrapped around it, similar to a goblet hold. The position forces an extremely upright torso, builds strong core engagement, and emphasizes the quads. It is a solid choice for lifters who lack the wrist mobility for a standard front squat rack.

en: Stand a barbell on end and hug it to your chest with both arms wrapped around it.
Hold the bar vertically against your chest with elbows tucked tight.
Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
Brace your core hard and lift your chest.
Squat down by sitting back and bending your knees.
Maintain an upright torso to keep the bar pressed to your chest.
Descend until your thighs are parallel to the floor or deeper.
Drive up through your heels to return to standing.
Forces upright torso for safer squat mechanics
Builds strong core engagement
Emphasizes quad development
Alternative for lifters with wrist mobility issues
Strong arm and grip workout from holding the bar
Easier to learn than the standard front rack position

description.en: The barbell front raise and pullover is a compound exercise where you lie on a bench, start with the bar at your hips, arc it overhead (front raise), then continue the arc behind your head (pullover), and reverse back to your hips. It combines shoulder flexion with lat/chest extension in one continuous movement.

en: Lie on a flat bench holding a light barbell with an overhand grip at your hips, arms extended.
Keeping arms straight, raise the bar in an arc from your hips up and over your head (front raise phase).
Continue the arc behind your head, lowering the bar toward the floor behind you (pullover phase).
Feel the stretch through your lats and chest at the bottom of the pullover.
Reverse the motion — pull the bar back up and over, arcing from behind your head back to your hips.
That is one complete rep.
Keep your arms straight (slight elbow bend) throughout the entire arc.
Use light weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps. Move slowly with control.
Combines front raise and pullover in one movement
Builds shoulder flexibility and strength
Stretches the chest and lats
Unique compound exercise
Excellent for shoulder mobility
Time-efficient

description.en: The barbell incline reverse grip spider curl with chest support is a strict spider curl done with a reverse grip on a barbell. The lifter lies face down on an incline bench and curls with palms down. The reverse grip biases the brachialis and forearms.

en: Set an incline bench at about forty five degrees.
Lie face down on the bench with chest supported.
Hold a barbell with a shoulder width reverse grip.
Let the arms hang straight down.
Brace your core and keep the chest pressed.
Curl the bar up toward the shoulders.
Squeeze the brachialis hard at the top.
Lower with control to a full extension.
Trains the brachialis
Builds the forearms
Strong reverse grip variation
Strict chest supported form
Useful for arm size

description.en: The battling ropes power slam is a battle rope drill that lifts both rope ends overhead and slams them down forcefully. The full body slam loads the lats, shoulders, and core. It is a brutal conditioning move.

en: Grip both battle rope ends with the arms at the sides.
Stand with the feet shoulder width apart facing the anchor.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lift both rope ends overhead together.
Slam the rope ends down to the floor in front of you.
Use the lats and core in the slam.
Pick the ropes back up immediately.
Continue slamming for the working set.
Burns calories fast
Builds full body power
Strong conditioning move
Trains the lats
Useful for athletes
Builds explosive power

description.en: The bottle weighted armpit row uses weighted bottles or jugs to perform a high pull where the elbows lead up to the armpits. The pattern targets the side delts, upper traps, and rhomboids with simple home equipment. It is a great alternative to the upright row.

en: Stand tall holding a weighted bottle in each hand at the front of your thighs.
Set your feet at shoulder-width and brace your core.
Keep the bottles close to your body throughout.
Pull the elbows up and out to the sides toward your armpits.
Lead the motion with the elbows above the hands.
Stop when the elbows reach armpit height.
Pause briefly and squeeze the upper back.
Lower the bottles back to the start with control.
Targets side delts and traps
No dumbbells required
Easy to scale at home
Builds shoulder width
Travel-friendly setup
Useful upright row swap

description.en: The bottle weighted overhead crunch is a sit up variation with the load held overhead. The lifter lies on the back and holds a water bottle overhead with both hands. The lifter crunches up keeping the bottle reaching for the ceiling. The overhead load adds resistance to the abs.

en: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent.
Hold a filled water bottle with both hands.
Extend the arms overhead behind the head.
Brace your core hard.
Keep the bottle overhead as you crunch up.
Lift the upper body off the floor while reaching the bottle to the ceiling.
Squeeze the abs at the top.
Lower back down with control.
Strong abs builder
Adds overhead load to crunches
Easy at-home weighted move
Trains long lever abs
Builds core strength
No gym needed

description.en: The cable lying fly is a chest fly performed lying on a flat bench positioned between two low cable pulleys. The cables provide constant tension throughout the fly, unlike dumbbells which lose tension at the top. It is one of the best exercises for constant-tension chest isolation.

en: Set two cable pulleys to their lowest position. Place a flat bench between them.
Lie on the bench. Grip a D-handle in each hand.
Start with arms extended above your chest, slight elbow bend, palms facing each other.
Lower both arms out to the sides in a wide arc, maintaining the slight elbow bend.
Lower until you feel a deep stretch across your chest.
Pull the handles back together above your chest by squeezing your pecs.
Squeeze at the top — the cables maintain tension here unlike dumbbells.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Constant cable tension throughout — even at the top
Superior to dumbbell fly for constant tension
Deep chest stretch at the bottom
Easy to load progressively
Excellent for chest hypertrophy
Joint-friendly with controlled loading

description.en: The cable standing up straight crossover is a chest isolation exercise performed between two cable pulleys set at shoulder height. Standing upright with the cables pulling directly from the sides, the straight-across pull path targets the mid-chest evenly. It is a classic cable station exercise for building chest definition.

en: Set both cable pulleys to roughly shoulder height. Attach a D-handle to each.
Grip one handle in each hand. Step to the center and stagger your stance for stability.
Start with arms out to the sides at shoulder height, palms forward, cables taut.
Set a slight elbow bend and lock it throughout.
Bring both handles together in front of your chest in a wide arc. Keep your torso upright — do not lean forward.
Squeeze your chest hard when the handles meet. Hold one second.
Slowly let the handles travel back out under control. Feel the stretch in your chest.
Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Targets the mid-chest evenly with constant cable tension
Upright torso eliminates lower-back involvement
Peak contraction at center with a deep stretch at the sides
Easy to adjust pulley height for upper or lower chest bias
Excellent finisher for chest workouts
Easy to load progressively

description.en: The calf stretch with hands against the wall is a classic standing calf stretch. With the hands on the wall and one foot stepped back, pressing the heel down lengthens the calves and Achilles.

en: Stand facing a wall about an arm length away.
Place both hands on the wall at shoulder height.
Step one foot back keeping the leg straight.
Plant the back heel firmly on the floor.
Bend the front knee and lean toward the wall.
Feel the stretch in the back calf and Achilles.
Keep the back heel pressed down throughout.
Hold the stretch for the desired duration then switch sides.
Lengthens the calves and Achilles tendon.
Improves ankle mobility.
No equipment needed beyond a wall.
Easy to perform anywhere.
Carryover to squat depth and running mechanics.
Reduces calf tightness.

description.en: Crescent Moon Pose is a standing yoga side stretch where you stand tall, reach both arms overhead, and lean to one side, creating a crescent shape with the body. It stretches the obliques, intercostals, and lats while opening the side body. It is one of the simplest and most accessible side-stretching yoga poses.

en: Stand tall in Mountain Pose with feet together or hip-width apart.
Reach both arms straight overhead. Clasp your hands together with index fingers extended (or grip one wrist).
Engage your core. Press your feet firmly into the floor.
Lean your upper body to the right by bending at the waist. Keep your hips facing forward and level.
Feel the stretch through your left side body — obliques, lats, and intercostals.
Look up under your top arm or straight ahead.
Hold for 5 to 8 breaths. Breathe deeply into the stretched side.
Return to center on an inhale and switch sides.
Stretches the obliques, lats, and intercostals
Opens the side body and improves lateral flexibility
Improves breathing capacity by opening the rib cage
Energizing and accessible to all levels
No equipment needed
Quick stretch that can be done anywhere

description.en: The crunch hold lifts into the top of a crunch and holds the position for time rather than performing reps. The sustained isometric contraction builds ab endurance and mind-muscle connection.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Hands behind your head or across your chest.
Crunch up — lift your shoulders off the floor.
Hold the top crunch position. Squeeze your abs continuously.
Hold for 15 to 30 seconds (or as long as possible).
Lower slowly when you can no longer maintain the position.
Rest and repeat for 3 to 5 sets.
Build up hold time progressively.
Keep your lower back pressed into the floor.
Builds ab endurance through isometric hold
Develops mind-muscle connection
No movement — pure sustained tension
No equipment needed
Useful for core endurance
Beginner-friendly

description.en: The dip on floor with chair is a bench dip done with a chair as the support. The lifter places the hands on the chair seat behind and dips down. It is a useful at-home tricep builder.

en: Sit on the floor in front of a sturdy chair.
Place the hands on the seat behind you.
Extend the legs out in front and lift the hips off the floor.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lower the hips down by bending the elbows.
Stop when the elbows reach about ninety degrees.
Press through the palms to lock the elbows.
Continue for the working set.
Trains the triceps
Strong home option
Builds the chest
Useful for travel
Builds the upper arms
No real equipment needed

description.en: The dumbbell Bulgarian split squat is a single-leg squat performed with the back foot elevated on a bench and a dumbbell in each hand. The elevated rear foot forces the front leg to do nearly all the work, building tremendous quad and glute strength on each side independently. It is one of the best exercises for fixing left-right imbalances and developing serious single-leg strength.

en: Stand roughly two to three feet in front of a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides.

Place the top of your right foot (laces down) on the bench behind you. Your left foot is planted flat on the floor, far enough forward that when you lunge down, your left shin stays close to vertical.
Stand tall with chest up and core braced. Pull your shoulders back.
Lower your body straight down by bending the front (left) knee. Your back (right) knee should travel down toward the floor.
Descend until your front thigh is roughly parallel to the floor. Your back knee should approach the floor without slamming into it.
Drive through your front foot to push back up to the starting position.
Complete all reps on the left leg, then switch and elevate your left foot to work the right leg.
Keep your torso mostly upright. A slight forward lean is acceptable but avoid hunching.
Builds the quads and glutes one leg at a time with strict form
Exposes and aggressively corrects left-right strength imbalances
Heavy quad and glute stimulus with light loads
Trains balance, ankle stability, and core control
Lower spinal load than back squats while training similar muscles
Excellent for athletes — high carryover to sprinting and jumping

description.en: The dumbbell rotational grip bench press starts at the bottom with a neutral grip (palms facing each other) and rotates to a pronated grip (palms forward) at the top of each rep. The rotation activates more chest fibers and reduces shoulder strain at the bottom while still building pressing strength.

en: Lie on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand at chest level.
Start with palms facing each other (neutral grip), elbows tucked toward your sides.
Press the dumbbells up while gradually rotating your wrists outward.
At the top, your palms should face forward (pronated grip) with arms fully extended.
Squeeze your chest hard at the lockout.
Lower the dumbbells back down while reversing the rotation.
Return to the neutral grip with elbows tucked at the bottom.
Maintain control through the rotation throughout the entire range of motion.
Combines neutral and pronated grip benefits in one rep
Reduces shoulder strain at the bottom position
Increases chest activation through the rotation
Variable grip pattern engages more muscle fibers
Joint-friendly pressing variation
Excellent for shoulder issues at full pronation

description.en: The dumbbell seated one arm front raise is a strict front shoulder isolation move performed seated with one arm at a time. The seated position eliminates leg drive and lower back swing. The unilateral approach allows full focus on each front delt and helps fix side-to-side imbalances.

en: Sit on a bench with your back upright and feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in one hand resting on your thigh.
Keep your other hand on the bench or your hip for support.
Brace your core and keep your back flat.
Raise the dumbbell straight in front of you with a slight bend in the elbow.
Lift until the arm is parallel to the floor.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower slowly back to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Isolates the front deltoid
Removes leg and lower back drive
Builds front shoulder definition
Allows unilateral focus
Helps fix side-to-side imbalances
Reduces cheating and momentum

description.en: The dumbbell seated single arm front raise isolates each front deltoid in a strict seated position. The seated setup removes leg drive and most torso swing. Working one arm at a time allows full focus on the working delt and also lets you brace harder for tougher reps.

en: Sit upright on a bench with feet flat on the floor.
Hold a dumbbell in one hand at your side or resting on your thigh.
Keep your other hand braced on the bench.
Brace your core and keep your back flat.
With a slight bend in the elbow, raise the dumbbell straight in front of you.
Lift until your arm is parallel to the floor.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower with control. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Isolates each front deltoid
Strict, swing-free shoulder work
Builds front shoulder definition
Helps fix side-to-side imbalances
Allows heavier focus on the working arm
Reduces cheating and momentum

description.en: The dumbbell single arm neutral grip front raise is a unilateral front raise with a neutral palm grip. The lifter holds a dumbbell with a hammer grip and lifts it straight up in front to shoulder height. The neutral grip emphasizes the front delt.

en: Stand tall with a dumbbell in one hand at the side.
Grip the dumbbell with a neutral palm facing the body.
Brace your core and set the chest tall.
Keep the arm slightly bent throughout.
Raise the dumbbell straight up in front.
Stop when the dumbbell reaches shoulder height.
Pause briefly at the top.
Lower the dumbbell back to the side with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Strong front delt builder
Trains the upper chest
Strong unilateral focus
Easy to scale loading
Useful shoulder builder
Strong dumbbell move

description.en: The dumbbell standing tricep extension holds a single dumbbell with both hands overhead and lowers it behind the head by bending at the elbows. The overhead position stretches the long head of the tricep for maximum activation.

en: Stand tall. Hold a dumbbell with both hands overhead, arms extended. Grip the inner plate.
Keep upper arms vertical, pointing to the ceiling.
Bend at the elbows to lower the dumbbell behind your head.
Lower until you feel a deep tricep stretch.
Extend your elbows to press back to lockout.
Squeeze your triceps at the top.
Keep elbows pointing up — do not let them flare forward.
Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Targets the long head of the tricep
Overhead position maximizes long-head stretch
Simple single-dumbbell setup
Builds tricep size and strength
Easy to load progressively
Classic tricep exercise

description.en: The dumbbell standing wrist curl is a forearm isolation exercise where you curl dumbbells up and down using only the wrists, with the forearms held still. The exercise targets the forearm flexors directly, building grip strength and visible forearm size. It is a simple, accessible accessory for any arm or forearm-focused workout.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing your body.
Rotate your wrists so your palms face forward. The dumbbells now hang in front of your thighs.
Pin your upper arms against your sides — they should not move during the exercise.
Allow the dumbbells to roll down to the tips of your fingers as you let your wrists extend backward (knuckles forward).
Curl the dumbbells back up by flexing only at the wrists. Squeeze the dumbbells back into your palms as you curl up.
Continue until your wrists are fully flexed (palms angled toward your forearms). Squeeze the forearms hard for one second at the top.
Slowly extend your wrists back to the start position over a count of two seconds.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a light to moderate weight; reps should be in the 12 to 25 range.
Direct isolation of the forearm flexors
Builds grip strength and visible forearm size
Easy to do at home with one pair of dumbbells
Useful accessory for any pulling exercise
Carries over to deadlifts, rows, and pull-ups
Easy to scale by changing weight

description.en: The elevated standing calf raise performs bodyweight calf raises while standing on a step, block, or stair edge. The elevation allows the heels to drop below the step level, providing a full stretch that flat-floor calf raises cannot achieve.

en: Stand with the balls of your feet on a step edge. Heels hanging off.
Hold a wall or railing for balance.
Lower your heels as far as possible for a deep calf stretch.
Press through the balls of your feet to raise as high as possible.
Squeeze your calves at the top.
Lower under control. Full range every rep.
Aim for 20 to 30 reps with bodyweight.
Add dumbbells for progressive overload.
Full range of motion from step elevation
Deep calf stretch at the bottom
No weights needed for effective training
Available on any staircase
Builds calf size and strength
Easy to add weight with dumbbells

description.en: The good morning squat combines a good morning (hip hinge) with a squat in one continuous movement. You hinge forward into a good morning, then from the bottom position, sit into a squat, then stand. It builds both hinge and squat patterns in one exercise.

en: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hands behind your head or at your chest.
Hinge at the hips — push your butt back, lowering your torso forward (good morning).
At the bottom of the hinge, bend your knees and sit into a squat.
From the squat bottom, stand up by extending hips and knees.
That is one rep. Continue flowing: stand → hinge → squat → stand.
Maintain a flat back during the hinge portion.
Move smoothly between patterns.
Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Trains both hinge and squat patterns
Builds hamstring, quad, and glute strength
Time-efficient compound movement
Develops pattern transitions
No equipment needed
Useful for warm-up or conditioning

description.en: The hyperextension (also called the back extension) is a posterior-chain exercise performed on a 45-degree or horizontal hyperextension bench. With the hips supported by the pad, you hinge down and back up using the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back muscles. It is one of the best exercises for building lower-back strength and is widely used as both a warm-up and an accessory lift.

en: Set up on a 45-degree hyperextension bench. Adjust the pad so it sits just below your hip bones, with your feet locked under the foot pads.
Cross your arms over your chest or place your hands behind your head. Brace your core.
Start with your torso angled up so your body forms a roughly straight line from heels to head.
Hinge forward at the hips by lowering your torso toward the floor. Keep your back flat — do not round.
Lower until your torso is roughly perpendicular to the floor or until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings.
Reverse the movement by squeezing your glutes and hamstrings to bring your torso back up.
Stop at the position where your body forms a straight line. Do not hyperextend (overarch) the lower back at the top.
Repeat for the desired number of reps. Add load by holding a weight plate against your chest as you get stronger.
Builds the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings
Excellent rehabilitation and warm-up exercise
Builds endurance in the spinal erectors
Easy to scale by adding load
Improves the hip-hinge pattern
Useful accessory for the deadlift and squat

musclesWorked: Trapezius and rhomboids (when hands behind head)

description.en: The inverted shrug (scapula pull-up or hanging scapula depression) hangs from a pull-up bar with straight arms and performs scapular depression — pulling the shoulder blades down without bending the elbows. It builds lower trap strength and scapular control, essential for pull-up mechanics.

en: Hang from a pull-up bar with straight arms, overhand grip.
Start in a passive hang — shoulders shrugged up near your ears.
Without bending your elbows, pull your shoulder blades down and back (depress).
Your body will rise 1 to 2 inches. Squeeze your lower traps.
Release back to passive hang.
Continue for the desired reps.
This is a small but important movement.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Builds lower trap strength
Develops scapular depression control
Essential for proper pull-up mechanics
Prevents shoulder injury during hanging
Simple concept with big carryover
Useful warm-up before pull-ups

description.en: The kettlebell lying on floor chest press is a floor press performed with two kettlebells from a back-down position. The floor stops the elbows at a safe range and removes the bottom portion of the press. The kettlebell offset weight forces extra grip and stabilizer work.

en: Lie on the floor with a kettlebell in each hand at chest level.
Bend your knees with feet flat on the floor.
Hold the kettlebells with palms facing each other and elbows tucked.
Brace your core and pin your shoulder blades down.
Press both kettlebells straight up over your chest.
Lock out the elbows at the top.
Lower with control until the back of your upper arms touch the floor.
Reset and press up for the next rep.
Builds chest and triceps
Floor stops at safe range
No bench needed
KB grip challenge
Trains stabilizers
Travel-friendly

description.en: The kettlebell one-arm push press is an overhead pressing variation where you use a slight knee dip and leg drive to help press a single KB overhead. The leg assist allows heavier loading than the strict press while still building shoulder strength.

en: Clean a KB to the right front rack.
Stand tall. Feet hip-width apart.
Dip slightly by bending your knees (3 to 5 inches).
Drive explosively through your legs while pressing the KB overhead.
Lock out at the top.
Lower the KB back to the rack under control.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Use heavier weight than strict press but lighter than jerks.
Allows heavier overhead loading than strict press
Builds overhead strength with leg assist
Develops timing between legs and shoulders
Easier to learn than the jerk
Excellent for building pressing volume
Unilateral — exposes imbalances

description.en: The kettlebell sit up press combines a full sit-up with an overhead press at the top. Lying on your back with a kettlebell at your chest, you sit up and press the kettlebell overhead at the peak position. The combo trains the abs through the sit-up and the shoulders through the press in one rep.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Hold a kettlebell at your chest with both hands.
Brace your core and engage your abs.
Sit up by curling your torso off the floor toward your knees.
At the top of the sit-up, press the kettlebell straight overhead.
Lock out your arms with the kettlebell directly above your shoulders.
Lower the kettlebell back to your chest.
Lie back down with control while keeping the kettlebell against your chest.
Trains abs and shoulders in one rep
Builds strong sit-up strength
Develops shoulder strength under core fatigue
Time-efficient compound combo
Strong functional carryover
Easy to scale by changing kettlebell weight

description.en: The kettlebell standing bottoms up one arm shoulder press is a stability press performed standing tall with the bell inverted. The bottoms up position demands constant grip pressure and refined shoulder control.

en: Stand tall with feet hip width apart.
Hold a kettlebell upside down at the rack with the bell above the wrist.
Squeeze the handle hard to keep the bell balanced.
Brace the core and lock the rib cage down.
Press the kettlebell straight up to lockout overhead.
Keep the wrist neutral and the bell perfectly vertical.
Lower the kettlebell back to the rack with full control.
Complete all reps on one side then switch arms.
Demands elite grip and forearm strength.
Builds shoulder stability under unstable overhead load.
Trains the core and obliques to resist tipping.
Improves rotator cuff control and shoulder health.
Sharpens mental focus through the unstable bell.
Excellent shoulder activation for warm ups.

description.en: The kipping handstand push-up uses a hip kip (explosive hip extension) to assist the pressing phase of a handstand push-up. It allows higher rep output than strict HSPUs and is commonly used in CrossFit workouts.

en: Kick up into a wall-supported handstand. Hands about shoulder-width apart.
Lower your head toward the floor by bending at the elbows.
At the bottom, tuck your knees slightly toward your chest.
Explosively extend your hips and legs upward while pressing with your arms.
The hip kip assists the pressing phase.
Lock out at the top.
This allows more reps than strict HSPUs.
Master strict HSPUs first for shoulder safety.
Higher rep output than strict HSPUs
Develops overhead pressing endurance
CrossFit competition exercise
Builds explosive pressing power
Develops kipping mechanics
Conditioning benefit from high rep sets

description.en: The kneeling forward hip circles is a hip mobility drill done on all fours. The mover lifts one knee and circles it forward to mobilize the hip joint. It is a useful warm-up drill for the hips before training.

en: Set up on hands and knees in a quadruped position.
Place the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips.
Brace your core and keep the back flat.
Lift one knee out to the side.
Circle the knee forward toward the hand.
Continue the circle back to the start position.
Maintain a steady tempo.
Finish all reps then switch sides.
Mobilizes the hips
Strong warm-up drill
Useful before training
Builds hip range
Activates the glutes

description.en: The overhead clap is a simple mobility drill where you stand tall and bring both arms up overhead to clap your hands together. It mobilizes the shoulders, activates the lower traps and serratus anterior, and is one of the simplest warm-up exercises for the upper body.

en: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms at your sides.
Quickly raise both arms straight out to the sides and continue lifting them overhead.
Clap your hands together overhead.
Lower your arms back down to your sides under control.
Repeat for 15 to 25 reps.
Move at a moderate pace. The point is to mobilize and warm up the shoulders.
Keep your core braced and torso upright throughout.
Excellent warm-up before any upper-body training.
Mobilizes the shoulders dynamically
Activates the lower traps and serratus anterior
Improves shoulder warm-up before pressing
No equipment needed
Builds shoulder endurance
Easy to scale by adjusting tempo

description.en: The posterior neck isometric is a static neck strength move where the lifter presses the back of the head into the hands or a wall. The hands provide resistance while the neck extensors push back. The isometric hold builds neck strength safely.

en: Sit or stand tall with the spine neutral.
Place both hands on the back of your head.
Brace your core and keep the chin slightly tucked.
Push the back of the head back into the hands.
Resist the push with the hands at the same intensity.
Hold the static contraction without movement.
Breathe normally throughout the hold.
Release the press slowly.
Builds neck strength safely
Static isometric hold
No equipment needed
Useful for athletes
Strong neck builder
Easy to scale intensity

description.en: The prisoner half sit up is a partial range sit up with the hands clasped behind the head. The lifter sits up only halfway, keeping the lower back on the floor. The half range is a useful regression that protects the lower back while training the abs.

en: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor.
Place the hands behind the head with elbows out wide.
Brace your core hard.
Curl the upper body off the floor.
Sit up only halfway keeping the lower back on the floor.
Squeeze the abs at the top of the half sit up.
Pause briefly at the contracted position.
Lower back to the start with control.
Beginner friendly abs move
Protects the lower back
No equipment needed
Builds the abs
Useful core builder
Easy to scale

description.en: The resistance band side walk is functionally identical to the resistance band lateral walk — a glute activation drill where you place a band around your thighs or ankles and step laterally. The band tension forces the gluteus medius to work continuously to maintain hip width.

en: Place a mini band around your thighs (above the knees) or ankles for more difficulty.
Stand in a quarter-squat position — hips back, knees bent, feet hip-width apart.
Push your knees outward to load the band tension.
Step your right foot to the right side. Maintain band tension.
Step your left foot to follow, returning to hip-width.
Continue stepping right for the desired distance (10 to 20 steps).
Step back to the left for the same distance.
Keep your hips low. Knees pushed out throughout.
Maximally activates the gluteus medius
Excellent warm-up for squats and lunges
Improves knee tracking and hip stability
Helps prevent knee valgus
Highly portable
Easy to scale by changing band thickness

description.en: The reverse push-up is another name for the inverted row — you lie face up under a bar, grip it, and pull your chest toward the bar. It is the pulling counterpart to the push-up and builds back, rear delt, and bicep strength.

en: Set a bar at hip height in a rack. Lie face up underneath it.
Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart.
Extend your body in a straight line from heels to head.
Pull your chest toward the bar by driving your elbows back.
Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top.
Lower under control.
Adjust body angle for difficulty — more horizontal is harder.
Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Bodyweight pulling exercise — opposite of push-up
Builds back, rear delt, and bicep strength
Adjustable difficulty by body angle
No specialized equipment needed
Develops pulling strength
Excellent for beginners building toward pull-ups

description.en: The safety bar front squat uses a safety squat bar (SSB) held in the front rack position rather than the standard back position. The padded yoke and handles make the front-loaded position more comfortable than a standard barbell front squat while maintaining the upright torso and quad emphasis.

en: Set up a safety squat bar at front rack height in a rack.
Step under and position the bar across your front shoulders — the pads rest on your chest.
Grip the handles in front of you.
Unrack. Set feet shoulder-width apart.
Squat down while keeping an upright torso.
Descend to parallel or below.
Drive through your feet to stand.
The SSB handles make the front rack position much more comfortable than a barbell.
Comfortable front-loaded squatting
No wrist flexibility needed unlike barbell front squat
Maintains upright torso for quad emphasis
Padded yoke is comfortable
Useful for those with wrist or shoulder limitations
Builds quad and core strength

description.en: The shoulder grip pull-up is performed with hands placed at shoulder width using an overhand grip. The narrower-than-wide grip is shoulder-friendly and allows a strong contraction at the top. It hits the lats well and recruits the biceps more than a wide grip pull-up.

en: Reach up and grab a pull-up bar with an overhand grip.
Place your hands shoulder-width apart.
Hang from the bar with arms fully extended.
Brace your core and squeeze your shoulder blades down.
Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down and back.
Continue until your chin clears the bar.
Squeeze the lats hard at the top.
Lower with control to a full hang.
Shoulder-friendly grip width
Strong contraction at the top
Balanced lat and bicep recruitment
Builds back and arm strength
Useful for pull-up training
Improves grip strength

description.en: The Smith back wide shrug uses a Smith machine bar held behind the body with a wide grip for a shrug variation. The behind-the-back position with wide grip changes the angle of the shrug and adds rear delt and middle trap involvement compared to standard barbell shrugs.

en: Set up a Smith machine bar at thigh level.
Stand in front of the bar with the bar behind your legs.
Squat down and grip the bar with palms facing back, hands wider than shoulder-width.
Stand up with the bar held behind your body.
Position the bar against the back of your thighs.
Brace your core and pull your shoulders back.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Squeeze the traps hard at the top, then lower the bar back down with control.
Different angle than standard shrug
Builds upper traps and rear delts
Wide grip adds rear delt work
Smith machine allows safe loading
Strong shoulder blade retraction
Useful for trap training

description.en: The Smith wide shrug is performed with a wider than shoulder-width grip on the Smith machine bar. The wide grip activates more rhomboid and middle trap involvement than a standard shrug while the Smith machine fixed path eliminates balance demands. It builds full upper back development.

en: Set the Smith machine bar at hip level.
Stand under the bar with feet shoulder-width apart.
Grip the bar with a wide overhand grip, well outside the shoulders.
Unrack the bar and stand tall with arms straight.
Pull your shoulders back and brace your core.
Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears.
Hold the contraction at the top for one count.
Lower the bar back down slowly with control.
Wide grip increases middle trap and rhomboid engagement
Fixed bar path eliminates balance demands
Builds upper trap mass
Allows heavy progressive loading
Strong forearm engagement
Useful for hypertrophy training

description.en: The standing alternate arms circling is a shoulder mobility drill that uses big alternating arm circles. The mover circles one arm at a time in big controlled patterns. It is a useful warm-up drill for shoulders and posture.

en: Stand with the feet hip width apart.
Brace your core and keep the chest up.
Lift one arm overhead and the other to the side.
Begin circling one arm forward in a big arc.
As that arm comes down, lift the other to overhead.
Continue the alternating circles.
Use a steady controlled tempo.
Continue for the working set.
Mobilizes the shoulders
Strong warm-up drill
Useful before training
Builds shoulder range
Trains shoulder mobility

description.en: The suspended abdominal fallout is a powerful core move performed on suspension trainer straps. The lifter grips the handles and slowly falls forward into a long body extension. The straps force a brutal anti-extension challenge through the abs and lats.

en: Set a suspension trainer at chest height.
Grip the handles with hands shoulder-width apart.
Step the feet back and lean forward into the handles.
Brace your core hard and keep the body in a straight line.
Slowly fall forward extending the arms overhead.
Continue until the body is in a long extension.
Hold briefly with the abs braced.
Pull back to the start by squeezing the lats and abs.
Brutal anti-extension challenge
Builds strong abs
Trains lat strength
Strong functional core move
Useful core finisher
Strong rollout variation

description.en: The suspender star plank is a side plank variation with the bottom foot hooked into a suspension strap and the top arm and leg extended out in a star shape. The unstable strap and full extended position make for a maximum core stability challenge. It is an advanced oblique and total body stability exercise.

en: Adjust suspension straps to about a foot off the floor.
Place your right foot inside one strap.
Lie on your right side with body in a straight line.
Prop yourself up on your right forearm with elbow under shoulder.
Brace your core hard.
Lift your hips off the floor into a side plank.
Extend your left arm straight up toward the ceiling.
Lift your left leg up to form a star shape. Hold the position. Switch sides.
Maximum core stability challenge
Strong oblique engagement
Advanced side plank variation
Builds total body stability
Develops shoulder stability
Useful for advanced core training

description.en: The suspension hammer curl is performed gripping suspension straps with palms facing each other (hammer grip), then curling your body up by bending only at the elbows. The strap setup allows bodyweight bicep training that builds the biceps and brachialis with no weights required.

en: Anchor suspension straps overhead at a sturdy point.
Stand facing the anchor and grip the handles with palms facing each other.
Walk your feet forward so your body angles back with arms extended.
Set your feet shoulder-width apart on the floor.
Brace your core and stand tall.
Curl your body up toward the handles by bending only at the elbows.
Keep your upper arms locked in front of your body throughout.
Lower yourself back to the starting position with control.
Bodyweight bicep training
Hammer grip targets brachialis
Easy to scale by changing foot position
Builds bicep size with no weights
Excellent for home or travel training
Strong forearm engagement

description.en: The thoracic bridge is a dynamic mobility drill where you start in a reverse tabletop (face-up) position and rotate one arm under your body and back over to the opposite side, opening the chest and rotating the thoracic spine. It builds thoracic mobility, shoulder flexibility, and full-body coordination.

en: Sit on the floor with feet flat and knees bent. Place your hands behind you, fingers pointing back.
Lift your hips off the floor into a reverse tabletop position. Body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders.
Reach your right arm up and across your body to the left side. Let your hips rotate toward the left as you reach.
Continue until your right hand approaches the floor on the left side and your right hip drops to the floor.
Reverse the motion: lift your hips back up, sweep your right arm back over, and return to the starting reverse tabletop.
Repeat on the same side or alternate.
Move with control. The thoracic spine should rotate, not collapse.
Perform 5 to 8 reps per side.
Builds thoracic spine rotation under load
Opens the chest and shoulders
Develops full-body coordination
Trains the glutes and posterior chain isometrically
Excellent dynamic warm-up
No equipment needed

description.en: The weighted lying hip abduction is a side-lying leg lift performed with a weight plate or ankle weight on the top leg for loaded glute medius isolation. Lying on your side and lifting the top leg against gravity and added weight builds the gluteus medius for hip stability.

en: Lie on your right side with legs stacked. Place a weight plate on your left outer thigh or wear an ankle weight.
Support your head with your right hand. Left hand on the floor for stability.
Keeping your left leg straight, lift it upward toward the ceiling.
Lift to about 45 degrees. Squeeze your left glute medius.
Lower under control.
Complete reps, then switch sides.
Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Keep your hips stacked — do not let the top hip roll back.
Isolates the gluteus medius with added load
Builds hip stability
Easy to set up
Lying position eliminates momentum
Useful for rehab and prehab
Easy to scale with weight

description.en: The weighted seated triceps extension is a classic seated overhead tricep builder. The lifter sits on a bench, holds a single dumbbell overhead with both hands cupped under the top plate, and lowers it behind the head. It is a strong long head builder.

en: Sit on a bench holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands.
Cup the hands under the top inside plate.
Press the dumbbell overhead to lockout.
Brace your core and keep the chest tall.
Set the upper arms vertical pointing at the ceiling.
Lower the dumbbell behind the head by bending the elbows.
Stop when the elbows are fully bent.
Press back up to lockout squeezing the triceps.
Strong tricep builder
Trains the long head
Easy to scale loading
Builds tricep size
Useful arm builder
Strong dumbbell move
